content: Depression is a common condition during the postnatal period, and it can have significant negative effects on the infant, the family, and the mother herself. However, it remains unclear whether antidepressant medications are effective in preventing postnatal depression. Additionally, there is limited information about the potential adverse effects of these medications on both the mother and the infant, particularly during breastfeeding. This review is an update of a Cochrane Review that was last published in 2005. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of antidepressant medications in preventing postnatal depression. This was done by comparing antidepressants to other treatments, placebo, or standard care. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted on February 13, 2018, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Common Mental Disorders Controlled Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO. Additional searches were performed on the World Health Organization trials portal and ClinicalTrials.gov to identify unpublished or ongoing studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the initiation of antidepressants, either alone or in combination with other treatments, for the prevention of postnatal depression. Eligible participants were women who were either pregnant or had given birth within the previous six weeks and were not depressed at the start of the study. Two trials, involving a total of 81 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Both studies included women with a history of postnatal depression who were not taking antidepressants at the start of the trials. These studies were conducted by the same research group. The risk of bias was assessed as low or unclear in most areas for both studies. However, due to the small number of studies, a meta-analysis could not be performed. The first study compared the antidepressant nortriptyline with a placebo. The results showed no evidence that nortriptyline was effective in preventing postnatal depression. In this study, 23% of women taking nortriptyline (6 out of 26) and 24% of women taking placebo (6 out of 25) developed postnatal depression within the first 17 weeks postpartum (relative risk [RR] 0.96, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.36 to 2.59, very low-quality evidence). One woman taking nortriptyline experienced mania, and constipation was reported more frequently in the nortriptyline group compared to the placebo group. The second study compared the antidepressant sertraline with a placebo. In this study, 7% of women taking sertraline (1 out of 14) developed postnatal depression within the first 17 weeks postpartum, compared to 50% of women taking placebo (4 out of 8). However, it remains uncertain whether sertraline reduces the risk of postnatal depression (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.07, very low-quality evidence). One woman taking sertraline experienced a hypomanic episode. Dizziness and drowsiness were reported more frequently in the sertraline group compared to the placebo group. The conclusions of this review are limited by the small number of studies, the small sample sizes, and incomplete outcome data due to participant dropouts, which may have introduced bias. The certainty of the evidence was assessed as very low using the GRADE system. Furthermore, no data were available on secondary outcomes such as child development, the mother-infant relationship, breastfeeding, maternal daily functioning, family relationships, or maternal satisfaction. In conclusion, the current evidence base is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of antidepressants in preventing postnatal depression. It is notable that no new eligible trials have been conducted in the more than ten years since the last version of this review was published. Larger trials are needed to compare antidepressants with other preventive treatments, such as psychological interventions, and to examine potential adverse effects on the fetus or infant. Future research may also benefit from expanding the scope to include the prevention of perinatal depression (both antenatal and postnatal) and exploring the effects of continuing versus discontinuing antidepressants during pregnancy and the postpartum period.
